name: Ionized bracelets

lead: Ionized bracelets are wristbands, often silicone or metal, that are sold as emitting negative ions or 'balancing' the body. They sit in the same family as hologram and magnetic bands and are worn as both jewellery and a wellness accessory.

Their link to appearance is mainly as a worn accessory and through the confidence or well-being wearers attribute to them. Studies of related hologram bands and of air ionisation are described below; no published trial has tested ionized bracelets themselves.

paras: Worn on the wrist like any band, continuously or during sport. Makers describe the effect in terms of balance, energy or comfort.

Generally worn without direct physical harm. Regulators in several countries have ruled against comparable bracelet brands for unsupported performance claims, and consumers have received refunds in settlements.

chain: Wearer reports feeling more balanced or energetic
angle.text: Ionized bracelets are worn as a styling accessory. Wearers and sellers describe a sense of balance and energy; the appearance benefit is the accessory plus this self-reported confidence.

lead: Ionized bracelets are wrist accessories marketed as releasing negative ions or otherwise 'balancing' the body's energy. They are one of several wearable wellness bands, alongside hologram and magnetic bracelets, that are sold on style as well as claimed benefit.

People wear them as an accessory that is part of an outfit and as a personal-wellness item; proponents describe feeling more balanced or energetic. The look-related payoff is therefore mostly the accessory itself and the self-reported lift in well-being that wearers describe.
No published study was found that tests ionized bracelets specifically. Research on the closest products, hologram bracelets, and on air ionisation in general is summarised below [1][2].

paras: The bracelets are typically made of silicone or metal and are sold with the claim that they emit negative ions or otherwise influence the body's energy balance. They are generally sold without medical claims on the packaging, but with wellness wording.

The best-documented comparable product is the Power Balance hologram bracelet, promoted from 2006 and sold from 2007 with claims of improving athletic performance [1]. In 2010 an Australian regulatory panel ordered the company to drop claims it called false and misleading, the ACCC took action, and the company admitted misleading conduct [1]. Italy's antitrust authority fined the company 300,000 euros in December 2010 [1].

Independent tests, including a 2010 Independent Investigations Group test with an Olympian and 2011 trials, reported no difference between real and sham bracelets [1]. A US class action settled in 2011 with a refund offered, and the company filed for Chapter 11 protection in November 2011 [1].

A 2013 review and meta-analysis found weak evidence that high-level negative air ionisation was linked to lower depression scores and no consistent effect on anxiety, mood, relaxation, sleep or comfort [2]. Those studies used air ionisers, not wristbands.
No studies found on ionized bracelets. Studies of hologram bracelets reported no effects on balance, flexibility or strength beyond placebo [1].

timeline.event: Power Balance hologram bracelets go on sale [1].
Australian regulators and Italy's authority act against hologram bracelet claims [1].
Class action settlement and bankruptcy filing by Power Balance [1].
